binders: A natural number m and an arbitrary type Information.
A proof that m > 0, so each state has at least one of the m real components indexed by Fin m.
An integer-indexed sequence of cell-average vectors Uᵢ = cellAverages(i), with Uᵢ : Fin m → Real.
An integer-indexed sequence valueAtOrigin(i) : Fin m → Real specifying the value assigned exactly at x = 0 in the interface datum for interface i.
A solver solve that accepts left and right m-component states and returns an Information value.
A readout fluxFromInformation that converts Information into an m-component real flux vector.
A purported physicalInterfaceFlux assigning an m-component real vector to every ordered pair of left and right states.
hypotheses: The component count is positive: 0 < m.
The flux scaling factor is positive: 0 < fluxScale.
For every pair of m-component states left and right, fluxFromInformation(solve(left,right)) equals physicalInterfaceFlux(left,right) as an m-component vector.
conclusions: The proposition repeats the already assumed fact 0 < m.
The proposition repeats the already assumed fact 0 < fluxScale.
There exists an updated integer-indexed sequence of m-component cell averages.
For every integer interface i, the datum formed from Uᵢ₋₁ on x < 0, valueAtOrigin(i) at x = 0, and Uᵢ on x > 0 satisfies the two-sided Riemann-data predicate with left state Uᵢ₋₁ and right state Uᵢ.
For every interface i, the flux extracted from solve(Uᵢ₋₁,Uᵢ) equals physicalInterfaceFlux(Uᵢ₋₁,Uᵢ).

For every cell i, the updated state is Uᵢⁿᵉʷ = Uᵢ − fluxScale · (Fᵢ₊₁ − Fᵢ), where Fⱼ = fluxFromInformation(solve(Uⱼ₋₁,Uⱼ)). Equivalently, using the exact-flux hypothesis, Uᵢⁿᵉʷ = Uᵢ − fluxScale · (physicalInterfaceFlux(Uᵢ,Uᵢ₊₁) − physicalInterfaceFlux(Uᵢ₋₁,Uᵢ)).
mathematical_definitions: An m-component state is a function Fin m → Real.
For interface i, define the interface datum Rᵢ : Real → (Fin m → Real) by Rᵢ(x) = Uᵢ₋₁ if x < 0, Rᵢ(0) = valueAtOrigin(i), and Rᵢ(x) = Uᵢ if x > 0.
The Riemann-data predicate for data R with states U_L and U_R means only that R(x) = U_L for every x < 0 and R(x) = U_R for every x > 0. It imposes no condition at x = 0.
Define the computed interface flux Fᵢ = fluxFromInformation(solve(Uᵢ₋₁,Uᵢ)).
The assumed exact-flux condition says F(left,right) = physicalInterfaceFlux(left,right) for every ordered state pair, not merely for neighboring cell states.

The finite-volume-style update operator on an integer-indexed state U and edge flux F is update(λ,U,F,i) = Uᵢ − λ(Fᵢ₊₁ − Fᵢ), with vector addition, subtraction, and scalar multiplication performed componentwise.
Interface i lies between cells i−1 and i, so Fᵢ is the left-face flux of cell i and Fᵢ₊₁ is its right-face flux.
translation.proposition_plain_english: Let a positive number m of real state components be fixed on a bi-infinite integer-indexed cell lattice. At every interface i, form piecewise-constant Riemann initial data using the average in cell i−1 to the left of the origin, the average in cell i to the right, and an arbitrary separately supplied value at the origin itself. Suppose a solver produces some information from every left/right state pair, a flux can be extracted from that information, and this extracted flux is assumed to equal a given physical interface-flux function for every state pair. If the real flux scale is positive, then there exists an updated cell-average sequence obtained by the componentwise conservative flux-difference formula Uᵢⁿᵉʷ = Uᵢ − fluxScale(Fᵢ₊₁ − Fᵢ). For each interface, the constructed datum has the required left and right constant states, and the solver's extracted flux equals the stipulated physical interface flux.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The theorem does not derive exact physical fluxes from properties of solve. Exact equality of the extracted and physical fluxes for every pair of states is an explicit premise, and the interface-specific equality in the conclusion is only its specialization.
Information is completely arbitrary, and no relationship between its internal contents and a Riemann solution is required beyond the flux readout equality.

The physicalInterfaceFlux function is itself arbitrary. No underlying conservation-law flux, consistency condition such as F(U,U) = f(U), symmetry, continuity, entropy condition, or other physical axiom is supplied.

The constructed object Rᵢ is only Riemann initial data. The proposition does not construct or characterize the time-dependent solution of a Riemann problem, waves, wave speeds, shocks, rarefactions, or a Godunov state.
The Riemann-data predicate deliberately excludes x = 0. Therefore valueAtOrigin(i) is unconstrained, and the first conclusion holds for every choice of that value.
valueAtOrigin does not influence solve, either interface flux, or the updated cell averages; it is used only to fill the otherwise unconstrained origin value in Rᵢ.

The existential updatedCellAverages is obtained by direct definition from the supplied data. Its existence does not establish solvability, stability, convergence, accuracy, or regularity of a numerical scheme.
Although no uniqueness clause is stated, the pointwise update equality determines updatedCellAverages uniquely by function extensionality.

The update has a local conservative flux-difference form, with the same Fᵢ entering adjacent cells with opposite signs. The theorem does not state a global conservation result, and on the bi-infinite integer lattice such a result would require summability or finite-domain boundary assumptions.
fluxScale is only required to be positive. There is no upper bound, CFL restriction, decomposition into time-step and cell-width factors, or dimensional-consistency condition.
The grid is the full integer lattice. No finite boundary, boundary condition, nonuniform cell geometry, mesh width, or physical location of cells is represented.
The theorem describes a single algebraic update. It does not iterate time steps or prove preservation of admissibility, positivity, invariant regions, or any norm bound.
The result repeats 0 < m and 0 < fluxScale in its conclusion without strengthening them.
If m = 0 or fluxScale ≤ 0, the corresponding premise cannot be supplied, so the universally quantified implication is vacuous for those choices.
Positivity of m guarantees a nonempty component index, but the proposition makes no claim that the components correspond to particular conserved physical variables.
ambiguities: The name physicalInterfaceFlux carries no formal physical semantics beyond being an arbitrary function of two state vectors.
The name solve does not specify whether Information represents a full Riemann solution, sampled interface data, wave information, or merely an encoding sufficient for flux extraction.
fluxScale may be intended as a time-step-to-cell-width ratio, but the proposition represents it only as an arbitrary positive real scalar.
The orientation is fixed algebraically by interface i joining left cell i−1 to right cell i; no separate geometric orientation or flux normal is formalized.
The special origin value may reflect a convention for discontinuous initial data, but the proposition intentionally leaves it irrelevant to the Riemann predicate and all flux computations.
